On January 31, 2024, the Company completed the sale ("the 2024 Worldpay Sale") of a 55 % equity interest in its Worldpay Merchant Solutions business to private equity funds managed by GTCR, LLC (such funds, the "Buyer"). On January 9, 2026, FIS completed its previously announced (i) acquisition of the Issuer Solutions business (the "Issuer Solutions Business") from Global Payments Inc. ("Global Payments") (the "Issuer Solutions Acquisition") and (ii) sale of all of its equity interests in Worldpay (the "2026 Worldpay Minority Interest Sale"), pursuant to the transaction agreement (the "Transaction Agreement"), entered into on April 17, 2025, by and among FIS, Global Payments, Total System Services LLC, and Worldpay. FIS acquired the Issuer Solutions Business from Global Payments in exchange for FIS' minority interest in Worldpay and approximately $ 7.7 billion in cash, which is equal to the difference between the purchase price payable by FIS in respect of the Issuer Solutions Business and the purchase price payable by Global Payments in respect of FIS' minority interest in Worldpay. The cash payment amount is subject to customary post-closing adjustments in respect of the respective purchase price for each of Worldpay and the Issuer Solutions Business. The purchase price paid by Global Payments in respect of Worldpay was based on a $ 24.25 billion enterprise valuation of Worldpay, and the purchase price paid by FIS in respect of the Issuer Solutions Business was based on a $ 13.5 billion enterprise valuation of the Issuer Solutions Business, in each case, subject to customary adjustments for the cash, debt and working capital (relative to a target) of Worldpay and the Issuer Solutions Business, respectively, as of the closing of the transactions. We funded the Issuer Solutions Acquisition through a combination of approximately $ 7.7 billion of new debt and the 2026 Worldpay Minority Interest Sale. We continued to account for our non-controlling 45 % equity interest in Worldpay using the equity method of accounting through the closing date of the 2026 Worldpay Minority Interest Sale. Banking Industry Consolidation We expect continued consolidation within the banking industry, primarily in the form of merger and acquisition activity among financial institutions, which generally increases competition among financial technology providers. However, consolidation resulting from specific merger and acquisition transactions may be beneficial to our business. When consolidations of financial institutions occur, merger partners often operate systems obtained from competing service providers. The newly formed entity generally makes a determination to migrate its core and payments systems to a single platform. When a financial institution processing client is involved in a consolidation, we may benefit if the client retains our solutions and expands the use of them following the consolidation to support the newly combined entity. Conversely, we may lose revenue if our solutions are not chosen to support the newly combined entity. It is also possible that larger financial institutions resulting from consolidation may have greater leverage in negotiating terms or could decide to perform in-house some or all of the solutions that we currently provide or could provide. We seek to mitigate the risks of consolidations by offering other competitive solutions to take advantage of specific opportunities at the surviving company. Goodwill Impairment Goodwill is assessed for impairment annually in the fourth quarter and on an interim basis if events or changes in circumstances indicate that it is more likely than not that the fair value of a reporting unit is less than its carrying amount. Determining the fair value of a reporting unit requires significant management judgment regarding the valuation methodologies and assumptions used to estimate fair value, including assumptions about future operating performance, discount rates, market conditions and other factors. As discussed in Note 5 to the consolidated financial statements, we evaluated whether events or changes in circumstances indicated that the fair value of either our Banking or Capital Markets reporting unit as of September 30, 2026, may be less than its carrying value. Our assessment identified events and changes in circumstances that occurred during the quarter that could affect the estimated fair value of our reporting units, including primarily a continued decline in our share price and market capitalization, as well as a reduction in management's projections of Banking's operating and financial performance based on developments in the quarter. In light of these developments, we performed quantitative goodwill impairment tests of both reporting units as of September 30, 2026. Fair value was estimated using an equal weighting of the income approach and market approach. The income approach used discounted cash flow analyses based on management's most recent forecasts, including assumptions regarding projected revenue growth, operating margins, capital expenditures, working capital requirements and terminal growth rates. The discount rate applied in the analysis was also a significant valuation assumption. The market approach used EBITDA multiples derived from comparable publicly traded companies and other relevant market data, which were applied to projected financial results. Management believes that consideration of both approaches provides an appropriate estimate of fair value because each approach incorporates different valuation attributes and market participant perspectives. We also assessed the reasonableness of the aggregate estimated fair value of the reporting units by comparison to our market capitalization over a reasonable period of time, considering expected acquirer expense synergies and control premiums observed in historical transactions involving payments and financial technology companies. Based on these tests, we concluded that the estimated fair value of the Banking reporting unit, which had goodwill of $19.9 billion as of September 30, 2026, exceeded its carrying amount by approximately 7%, while the estimated fair value of the Capital Markets reporting unit, which had goodwill of $5.1 billion as of that date, exceeded its carrying amount by more than 50%. Accordingly, no goodwill impairment charge was recognized. Determining the fair value of a reporting unit is subject to uncertainty as it is reliant on estimates of cash flows that extend far into the future, and, by their nature, are difficult to estimate over such an extended time frame. The estimated fair values of the reporting units are sensitive to changes in management's judgments and estimates, including projected revenue growth, operating margins, capital expenditures, working capital requirements, discount rates and market valuation multiples. In applying the income approach for the Banking reporting unit, we used a discount rate of 11.5%, based on the reporting unit's weighted average cost of capital, which incorporated a company-specific risk premium based on management's judgement as informed by market-based evidence and other relevant factors. Holding all other assumptions constant, an increase of approximately 75 basis points in the discount rate would have reduced the estimated fair value of the Banking reporting unit below its carrying amount under the income approach. In applying the market approach, a key assumption used is the EBITDA multiple. Holding all other assumptions constant, a decrease in the EBITDA multiple of greater than approximately 5% would 36 Table of Contents have reduced the estimated fair value of the Banking reporting unit below its carrying amount under the market approach. Given that the estimated fair value of the Banking reporting unit exceeded its carrying amount by approximately 7% as of September 30, 2026, relatively modest adverse changes in management's judgments and estimates, including projected revenue growth, operating margins, discount rates, and market valuation multiples, as well as further declines in our share price or market capitalization, further deterioration in Banking's operating performance, or unfavorable changes in macroeconomic or industry conditions would negatively affect the estimated fair value of the Banking reporting unit and could result in a future goodwill impairment charge, which could be material.
